newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: U.N. warns Cambodia on military spending, taxes.
newsitem.headline: U.N. warns Cambodia on military spending, taxes.

text.p: The United Nations warned Cambodia on Wednesday it is spending too much money on its security forces and failing to meet tax revenue collection targets.

It also said that international donors could not continue pouring aid into the country, a warning that came as some donor country diplomats in Phnom Penh suggested future aid might be linked to political stability.
A power struggle between the two leaders of Cambodia's deadlocked coalition government has led to increasing concern about stability and political violence in recent weeks.
"Too much of the country's resources continued to be allocated to non-productive military and police expenditures," the United Nations said in a statement released in Phnom Penh.
It also said tax collection was falling short of targets.
"It is neither realistic nor reasonable to expect the international community to substitute with its taxes for revenue which should be collected by Cambodia itself," it said.
The U.N. statement was to be delivered at a two-day Consultative Group meeting of bilateral and multilateral aid donors in Paris ending on Wednesday.
The meeting will determine Cambodia's aid budget for 1997.
Cambodia was hoping for $449 million this year as part of a $1.4 billion three-year aid package, finance ministry officials said.
International aid makes up nearly half of the annual national budget. Around half of annual government spending goes on defence and security.
The Cambodian army is fighting a low-intensity war with Khmer Rouge guerrillas while the feud between the county's two prime ministers has led to fears of more conflict.

The United Nations, which provided $88 million in aid in 1996, said sluggish tax collection and heavy spending on military and police forces were depriving health, education and agriculture programmes of funds.
But this year donors are considering linking aid to an improved political climate.
"There have been rumblings, especially from the Japanese and the Australians, on linking aid to political stability," a diplomat said.
The United Nations also said it was concerned about the wasteful exploitation of Cambodia's natural resources.
"We reiterate our deep concern...at the largely unmanaged and unplanned exploitation of Cambodia's rich endowment of forests and water," it said.
